reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Caused most often by gain-of-function variants in STIM1 or ORAI1, the key components of store-operated calcium entry; inheritance is usually autosomal dominant
Presents with slowly progressive proximal limb weakness, muscle cramps, myalgia, and exercise intolerance, often from childhood or early adulthood
STIM1 gain-of-function variants can cause Stormorken syndrome, a multisystem disorder combining myopathy with thrombocytopenia, bleeding tendency, miosis, and other features
Creatine kinase is often mildly to moderately elevated and electromyography shows a myopathic pattern

The defining biopsy feature is tubular aggregates, densely packed arrays of tubules derived from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, typically in type 2 fibres and best seen with oxidative and Gomori trichrome stains and electron microscopy
Tubular aggregates are a non-specific reaction pattern that also occurs in other conditions, so genetic and clinical correlation is needed
Assessment should include a platelet count and bleeding history given the Stormorken-syndrome association with STIM1 variants
Diagnosis combines the myopathic phenotype, tubular aggregates on biopsy, and STIM1 or ORAI1 genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Tubular aggregate myopathy arises from dysregulated store-operated calcium entry, the process by which depletion of sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium is sensed by STIM1 and triggers calcium influx through the ORAI1 channel. Gain-of-function variants in STIM1 or ORAI1 cause constitutive or excessive calcium entry, leading to calcium overload and abnormal proliferation and packing of sarcoplasmic reticulum membranes that form the characteristic tubular aggregates. Disturbed calcium homeostasis impairs muscle function, producing weakness, cramps, and exercise intolerance, and the same pathway abnormality accounts for the platelet and other systemic features of Stormorken syndrome.
additionalDifferentials: Metabolic myopathies with exercise intolerance and cramps
Other causes of tubular aggregates such as periodic paralysis or drug/toxin exposure
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy with oxidative enzyme and Gomori trichrome staining and electron microscopy to demonstrate tubular aggregates
Full blood count and bleeding assessment to detect thrombocytopenia in the Stormorken spectrum
Genetic testing of STIM1 and ORAI1 and a broader myopathy panel
redFlags: Bleeding tendency or thrombocytopenia suggesting Stormorken syndrome
Multisystem features such as miosis, asplenia, or ichthyosis in the STIM1 spectrum
Rapidly progressive weakness atypical for the usual slow course
Respiratory or cardiac involvement warranting evaluation
reference.prognosis: Muscle weakness typically progresses slowly and most patients remain ambulant, giving a generally favourable neuromuscular prognosis; in the Stormorken-syndrome end of the STIM1 spectrum, the bleeding tendency and multisystem involvement add to morbidity and require additional management.
pitfalls: Regarding tubular aggregates as diagnostic of a single disease when they are a non-specific reaction pattern
Missing the associated thrombocytopenia and bleeding risk of Stormorken syndrome in STIM1 disease
Overlooking a treatable alternative such as a metabolic myopathy or channelopathy
Failing to confirm the diagnosis genetically after finding tubular aggregates on biopsy
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
GeneReviews: STIM1- and ORAI1-related tubular aggregate myopathy and Stormorken syndrome
management: No disease-specific pharmacotherapy exists; management centres on tailored physiotherapy and graded low-impact exercise to preserve proximal strength and limit deconditioning
Symptomatic management of muscle cramps, myalgia and exercise intolerance with activity pacing
Occupational therapy, orthoses and mobility aids to maintain function and ambulation
Periodic monitoring of muscle strength and of respiratory and bulbar function as weakness progresses
In the Stormorken/STIM1 spectrum, surveillance for thrombocytopenia with bleeding precautions and platelet support around surgery or bleeding episodes
Genetic counselling given the usually autosomal dominant inheritance
